nodes.label: Grants.gov opportunity search
nodes.one_line: Find every live federal funding opportunity relevant to your field on Grants.gov and read its synopsis before it closes.
know_what: Grants.gov — the federal portal where discretionary federal opportunities are posted and applications submitted
Synopsis vs NOFO — the short search-result summary vs the full Notice of Funding Opportunity holding every requirement
Assistance Listing number (formerly CFDA) — the federal identifier that names the agency and program, and tells you whether an award is a grant or a cooperative agreement
Opportunity status — posted / forecasted / closed; forecasted listings can appear up to 12 months early as planning signals
Eligibility codes — who may apply (nonprofits, states, tribes, institutions of higher education), shown on the synopsis page
Funding amount and expected awards — the award ceiling, floor, and number of awards the agency intends to make
Cost-sharing and match flags — whether the NOFO requires a match, visible in the funding and eligibility sections
Closing-date rules — deadlines are in Eastern Time on the due date, and 'submitted' is not 'received' until Grants.gov validates the package
know_how: Search Grants.gov by keyword, agency, Assistance Listing, and opportunity status to surface live federal opportunities in your field
Open the synopsis first and read the eligibility, award amount, and closing date before downloading the full NOFO
Read the full NOFO's sections — program description, eligibility, application contents, review criteria, submission info — before deciding to apply
Check the forecasted opportunities quarterly so agencies' upcoming competitions appear on your calendar 6-12 months early
Confirm your SAM.gov registration and Grants.gov roles well before a deadline, since registration can take weeks
Verify the closing time and time zone against your calendar and submit 24-48 hours early to dodge portal outages
habits: Checking Grants.gov for your saved keyword set weekly, not only when a colleague forwards a link
Reading the synopsis and the Assistance Listing before the full NOFO, so deep reading goes only to real fits
Logging every opportunity you consider into the pipeline tracker with its number and closing date the day you find it
Keeping SAM.gov and Grants.gov registrations renewed so a live opportunity never expires while you register
Noting the forecasted competitions in your field so the calendar shows upcoming cycles before they post
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a one-page brief on a live Grants.gov opportunity — Assistance Listing number, agency, eligibility, award ceiling, closing date — from the synopsis alone, with no errors.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the synopsis as the announcement: the requirements live in the full NOFO, and applicants who skip it miss an eligibility or attachment rule and are rejected for compliance before their proposal is ever reviewed.
sources: Grants.gov — Search Grants and forecasted opportunities
2 CFR 200 (Uniform Guidance)
USASpending.gov — federal award data

nodes.label: Prior-awards research
nodes.one_line: Pull a foundation's IRS 990s and recent grants to see who they actually fund, at what size, and for what duration — not just what they claim to fund.
know_what: 990 vs 990-PF vs 990-EZ — the filings for public charities, private foundations, and small organizations, each with different grant-disclosure schedules
Schedule I — the part of a public charity's 990 that lists grants paid, to whom, and in what amounts
ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer — free, searchable digitized 990s and extracted grant records for U.S. nonprofits
Candid grant records — the foundation's grants as reported, searchable by recipient, subject, and geography
Grant size distribution — the median and range of a foundation's awards, which tells you whether your ask is realistic
Recurring grantees — organizations funded year after year, the signature of a relationship-driven giving pattern
Total giving and assets — the scale of the foundation from the 990's summary, which calibrates what share of its giving your ask would be
know_how: Pull the last two years of a foundation's 990s from ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer and read Schedule I for who was actually paid
Sort the grant list by size and by repeat recipient to find the foundation's real giving pattern, not its stated priorities
Check whether organizations like yours — type, geography, budget size — appear on the list, and at what dollar range
Compare the median grant against your planned ask; an ask several times the median is a signal to rescope or pass
Note multi-year vs one-year patterns and whether renewals happen, which shapes your relationship plan
Cross-check 990 data against Candid's grants view and the foundation's own annual report for the current year
habits: Reading the 990 before the website — the filing shows what they did, the site shows what they say
Checking Schedule I for actual recipients whenever a new foundation enters your pipeline
Tracking median grant size per foundation so every ask is calibrated before drafting
Flagging foundations whose 990 giving contradicts their stated focus, and trusting the 990
Recording grant-pattern notes on the funder record so the research compounds across proposals
nodes.checkpoint: From a foundation's last two 990s, state its total giving, median grant size, top three recipient types, and whether it funds organizations like yours — naming the Schedule I entries that support each claim.
nodes.common_failure: Researching the foundation's marketing materials instead of its 990s — the ask is sized to a stated mission that the actual grant list contradicts, and the proposal fails the program officer's 'does this look like us' test.
sources: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
IRS Form 990 and Schedule I instructions
Candid — Foundation Directory grant records

nodes.label: Opportunity watch
nodes.one_line: Run saved searches and alerts on Grants.gov, Candid, and state portals so new and recurring opportunities reach you instead of being missed.
know_what: Saved searches — stored Grants.gov query criteria that rerun automatically and email new matches
Grants.gov email notifications — daily or weekly digests of new postings matching your saved criteria
Candid funding alerts — saved subject and geography searches that email new foundation giving matches
State grant portals — state clearinghouses (e.g., the California Grants Portal) listing state agency opportunities separately from federal ones
Forecasted opportunities — federal competitions listed before the NOFO posts, the earliest warning of a cycle
Recurring cycles — foundations and agencies that open the same RFP on an annual or quarterly rhythm, predictable from last year's postings
Philanthropy News Digest — Candid's daily digest of new funding opportunities and announcements
know_how: Build a Grants.gov saved search from your working keyword set and turn on email notifications so new postings arrive without daily manual checks
Set a Candid alert for your subject and geography so foundation openings surface in your inbox
Subscribe to the newsletters and RFP pages of the 10-20 funders you already target, not just the directories
Maintain a 12-month calendar of known recurring cycles reconstructed from last year's postings and grantee reports
Triage alerts daily but act weekly: sort new matches into apply / watch / pass within seven days of posting
Re-run and refresh saved searches quarterly so stale keywords do not bury new opportunities
habits: Treating alerts as a triage queue, not an inbox — every match gets a fit call within the week
Keeping the saved-search keyword list in sync with the program's actual focus as it evolves
Recording the recurrence pattern of every funder you track: annual RFP, rolling, or quarterly board
Reviewing the alert setup monthly to kill dead searches and add new ones
Fixing the search when an alert misses a known posting, instead of just noting the miss
nodes.checkpoint: Set up working alerts on Grants.gov and Candid plus two funder newsletters, and for one week triage every alert into apply / watch / pass with a reason — with zero relevant opportunities missed that week.
nodes.common_failure: Subscribing to alerts and then ignoring them until the deadline passes — saved searches are only useful as a triage queue, and the unfiltered flood trains you to stop reading them.
sources: Grants.gov — saved searches and email notifications
Candid — funding alerts
Philanthropy News Digest (Candid)

nodes.label: Opportunity scoring
nodes.one_line: Score a live opportunity on fit, odds, and cost-to-apply, then make a defensible go/no-go call for your portfolio.
know_what: Fit score — your scored match on mission, geography, ask size, and eligibility against the funder's actual giving, not its website
Odds — the competition reality: applicants per award, e.g., NIH R01 success rates around 20-25% and many foundation grants 1 in 10-20 applicants
Cost-to-apply — the honest hours estimate (often 40-100 hours for a federal narrative, 8-20 for a foundation proposal) times your loaded staff rate
Capacity check — the number of proposals already in flight this quarter and whether the team can add one without degrading quality
Go/no-go threshold — the minimum combined score below which the opportunity is declined on purpose, set before scoring
Award value vs effort — dollars at stake divided by hours, the crude return that catches prestige chases
Review panel composition — federal panels of peer reviewers vs foundation staff, which changes how the proposal must read
know_how: Score each live opportunity on three axes — fit, odds, cost-to-apply — on 1-5 scales with definitions written down before scoring
Estimate odds from evidence: prior applicants vs awards in the NOFO or from the program officer, using published success rates (e.g., NIH R01 ~20-25%) where they exist
Estimate cost-to-apply from the outline: page count, boilerplate availability, data needs, and the revision loops a reviewer-grade draft requires
Run a weighted scorecard with fit dominant, and hold the go threshold fixed once the quarter's decisions are set
Compare against the portfolio: decline a 3.5-score opportunity if two stronger ones are already in flight
Record the score and the decision on the opportunity record so the reasoning survives the outcome
habits: Scoring every opportunity before writing a word, including the ones you are excited about
Deciding the go/no-go threshold once a quarter, not per opportunity, so it cannot be moved to fit a wish
Treating 'but it is prestigious' as a cost, not a benefit, in the scorecard
Re-scoring after reading the full NOFO, because synopses flatter fit
Reviewing past scores against actual outcomes to calibrate the odds estimate

know_why.claim: A weighted scorecard with a pre-set threshold beats gut feel for go/no-go decisions.
know_why.because: scoring forces fit, odds, and cost-to-apply to be priced separately and makes the decision reviewable after the outcome is known, whereas gut feel reliably overweights mission excitement and underweights odds and hours.
know_why.disputed_by: veteran grant developers who argue that experienced judgment reads the same evidence faster, and that scorecards manufacture false precision from odds estimates that are guesses either way.
know_why.source: Instrumentl and GrantStation go/no-go guidance; debate in Grant Professionals Association forums

nodes.checkpoint: Score a live opportunity on a weighted fit/odds/cost scorecard, make a go/no-go call against a threshold set before scoring, and write a two-sentence rationale that survives review after the outcome is known.
nodes.common_failure: Scoring after the decision: the scorecard is built to justify a yes the applicant already wanted, with the odds guess inflated — and the same 60 hours then go into a 1-in-30 shot.
sources: Instrumentl — opportunity scoring guidance
GrantStation — go/no-go decision resources
NIH — R01 success rate data (NIH Data Book)

nodes.label: Needs evidence
nodes.one_line: Find and cite the statistics, studies, and local data that quantify the problem you opened your statement with.
know_what: Authoritative sources — Census ACS, CDC BRFSS, Bureau of Labor Statistics, HUD's AHAR, USDA ERS food-security data — each with its own population and geography coverage
County Health Rankings & Roadmaps — the University of Wisconsin–Population Health Institute's county-level health data reviewers use to check local claims
Rates vs counts — a rate with a denominator (per 100,000) vs a raw count, and why reviewers distrust denominator-free numbers
Recency — the convention that need statistics sit within 3-5 years of submission, newer for fast-moving problems
Geographic match — national, state, county, or ZIP-level data, with the requirement that the figure matches your service area
Triangulation — two independent sources agreeing on a magnitude, which survives a reviewer's fact-check
Small-sample caveats — county-level rates with wide confidence intervals, which must be flagged rather than oversold
Meta-analyses and systematic reviews — the strongest evidence for prevalence and effect size, found via PubMed or the Cochrane Library
know_how: Find the federal or state source covering your population and geography, and pull the statistic with its year and table name
Step from national data down to state and county so the local gap is quantified, not asserted
Write every statistic with source and year in the draft ('per the 2022 ACS 5-year estimates…'), never bare
Check the denominator and population definition before citing — 'food insecure' means different things in USDA ERS vs Feeding America data
Verify the source year against the submission date and replace anything older than 5 years unless no newer data exists
Where local data is missing, cite the nearest proxy and say so, or plan primary data collection in the evaluation section
habits: Keeping a running evidence file of statistics with sources and years, captured as you read rather than at draft time
Fact-checking every statistic in the problem statement against its original table before submission
Preferring the primary source over the secondary article that quoted it
Asking 'does this number describe my population, or one that looks like it?' before citing
Re-verifying statistics when a proposal is reused a year later, because sources age out
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a need-evidence table for your problem statement with 5-10 statistics, each with primary source, year, geography, and population definition, and defend any local figure against a reviewer's fact-check.
nodes.common_failure: Citing a national statistic for a local claim, or a five-year-old figure with no year attached — one reviewer fact-check kills the credibility of the entire needs section.
sources: U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey
County Health Rankings & Roadmaps (University of Wisconsin–Population Health Institute)
Feeding America Map the Meal Gap
HUD Annual Homeless Assessment Report (AHAR)

nodes.label: Outcome measures
nodes.one_line: Choose indicators and data sources for each outcome so your proposal can claim measurable results, not intentions.
know_what: Indicator — the observable, countable proxy for an outcome, e.g., 'employment 6 months post-program' for 'sustained employment'
Baseline and target — the pre-program value and the numeric destination ('from 40% to 60%'), the minimum a measurable claim needs
Validated instruments — PHQ-9 for depression, GAD-7 for anxiety, the USDA 6-item Household Food Security Survey Module — measures with published reliability
Administrative data — records you already keep (attendance, enrollment, service logs) as low-burden indicators
Leading vs lagging indicators — early signals (session attendance) vs true outcomes (employment at 6 months)
Measurement burden — respondent and staff time per indicator, the hidden cost that sinks evaluation plans
Proxy indicators — the measurable stand-in when the real outcome cannot be measured directly (e.g., GPA for learning gains)
WIOA common measures — the federal employment-program indicators (employment rate, earnings, credential attainment) reviewers recognize
know_how: Write one indicator per outcome in the logic model, each with a data source and a collection method named
Set baseline and target from real data or a pilot, never from hope, and label the basis of each number
Choose a validated instrument where one exists for the outcome, and name the instrument in the proposal
Prefer administrative data over surveys where it answers the question — it costs less and cannot be gamed by self-report
Add one leading indicator per outcome so early results are visible before closeout
Cut any indicator whose measurement cost exceeds its value to the decision, and say why it was cut
habits: Asking 'how will we know?' for every outcome, and refusing 'we'll survey participants' as an answer without naming the instrument
Keeping baseline numbers attached to the objective they serve, so targets are never orphaned
Checking each indicator against the logic model: no indicator without an outcome, no outcome without an indicator
Piloting the measurement before the grant starts, because instruments fail in the field, not on the page
Treating a home-grown survey question as a last resort, never a default

know_why.claim: Outcome measures should be quantitative indicators with baselines and targets, even when the program's change is hard to count.
know_why.because: reviewers and closeout reports can only verify countable change, and a baseline-target pair is the difference between a claim and a number that can be checked.
know_why.disputed_by: evaluators in participatory and qualitative traditions (Most Significant Change, utilization-focused evaluation) who argue that numeric indicators flatten the outcomes that matter, and that well-collected qualitative evidence is more honest for complex programs.
know_why.source: W.K. Kellogg Foundation Evaluation Handbook; Michael Quinn Patton, Utilization-Focused Evaluation; Rick Davies & Jess Dart, The 'Most Significant Change' Technique

nodes.checkpoint: For a program with 3-5 objectives, produce a measure table naming the indicator, baseline, target, data source, collection method, and collection schedule for each — with every indicator traceable to a logic-model outcome.
nodes.common_failure: Indicators that measure activity ('we will track attendance') instead of outcome ('attendance rose 30%'), or targets with no baseline — the evaluation section then reports process, and the grantee cannot claim the change it promised.
sources: W.K. Kellogg Foundation Evaluation Handbook
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 validation literature (Kroenke et al.)
USDA Economic Research Service — Household Food Security Survey Module

nodes.label: Evaluation plan
nodes.one_line: Write the who-measures-what-when plan, with instruments and analysis, that turns outcome measures into a fundable evaluation section.
know_what: Formative vs summative evaluation — improvement feedback during the program vs a verdict on outcomes at the end
Process vs outcome evaluation — did implementation happen as designed vs did participants change
External evaluator — an independent contractor or university partner whose findings carry credibility internal staff lack
Evaluator credentials — relevant degrees, prior evaluation of similar programs, and experience with your population and methods
Logic model alignment — an evaluation plan that tests each outcome column of the model, the first thing reviewers check
Pre/post and comparison designs — measuring change within the group vs against a matched comparison group, with the tradeoff in confidence
W.K. Kellogg Foundation Evaluation Handbook — the standard reference funders recognize for writing evaluation sections
Evaluation budget — commonly 5-10% of a federal project budget, a line reviewers notice when it is missing
know_how: Write the evaluation section as who measures what, with which instrument, on what schedule, feeding which decision
Align the plan row by row to the logic model: every outcome column gets a measure, a method, and a use
Specify the design honestly — pre/post with its limitations stated, or a comparison group where the budget allows
Name the evaluator's role and credentials, or commit to hiring an external evaluator with stated qualifications
Budget evaluation explicitly at 5-10% of the project, with evaluator time and instrument costs itemized
Describe how findings will be used and shared — funders want evaluation that informs program decisions, not shelf reports
habits: Writing the evaluation plan from the logic model, not from a template, so measures and outcomes cannot drift apart
Discussing the evaluation with the would-be evaluator before the proposal is submitted, not after funding
Checking that every measure named in the plan is one the organization can actually collect with its staff and budget
Re-reading the plan asking 'what decision does this finding inform?' — a measure with no decision is dead weight
Treating evaluation as a budget line from the start, not an afterthought discovered at closeout

know_why.claim: An external evaluator is worth the budget for any outcome-level claim.
know_why.because: independent evaluators carry credibility with reviewers and funders, apply methodological distance internal staff cannot, and their findings survive scrutiny at closeout.
know_why.disputed_by: practitioners who argue that on small grants an external evaluator consumes 5-10% of the budget for reports nobody reads, and that internal evaluation with honest methods serves small programs better.
know_why.source: W.K. Kellogg Foundation Evaluation Handbook; debate in Grant Professionals Association and American Evaluation Association forums

nodes.checkpoint: Write an evaluation plan for a real proposal: design named, every logic-model outcome mapped to a measure and schedule, evaluator role and credentials stated, and a budget line of 5-10% that a reviewer could execute as written.
nodes.common_failure: A plan that names instruments but no schedule or owner — 'we will survey participants' with no baseline, no mid-point, and no named evaluator — which reviewers read as a promise the organization cannot keep.
sources: W.K. Kellogg Foundation Evaluation Handbook
CDC Framework for Program Evaluation in Public Health
American Evaluation Association — Guiding Principles for Evaluators
